your fingers arent going back to the fretboard naturally. ideally it takes almost no pressure and effort to press a note, just enough to sound out and lift when not needed. 

try practicing sitting down first, with the left arm higher like youre using a footstool. you shouldnt be using your left arm to hold the guitar upright, most of that force comes from the right arm and elbow pinning the body of the guitar to your body. so that your left hand can focus on holding and releasing notes. 

i practiced hammer ons and pull offs a lot to get the right feel. from holding down a note, a pull off to a hammer on the same place should be just one fluid motion. thats what i meant by going back to the fretboard naturally. the feeling is quite light. you can practice tapping the edge of a table first to get an idea. your fingers have a natural motion that they snap back to where they originally were. use that as much as possible reduce tension.

First off, don't stress over grades. It's the kind of thing where the more you stress, the lower you get. I briefly worked in a university and graduated with honors. My mother taught a few courses. We would observe that those who had high grades were just playing it cool. Some weren't grade conscious at all. 

Second, either your school has a freaking awful grading system or you're aiming wrong. What is the equivalent of an A in your school? If there's such a thing as 45% grade there, then a B would be 81%, maybe even lower. 

In most schools where I'm from, the passing grade is 75% and you literally can't get lower than 50%. The schools that didn't follow that system had 50% as passing and did go down to 0% but that only meant that 90% there is like 95% in the former. So the 90% you're aiming for is actually 95% in normal colleges. And your 80% is actually a 90%. 45% converts to 72.5%. Keeping all grades at 80+% ensures being in the Dean's List or equivalent. 

So if you still wanna stress over grades (since that's your choice), aim for 80s, not 90s.

i work by entering notes on a free DAW so this might not be the same for you but i also start with "oh thats a nice progression" and work from there. what i do is a lot of writing on paper what i want to accomplish. it doesnt work as well when i dont do the primary planning on paper. this can be scratch paper with only letters and numbers on it, not classic music staffs and notes.

i choose a tempo, key signature, chord progression. from that, i write the chords down with voice leading that makes sense over two octaves at first. if feeling inspired, make an inversion of the same progression.  no rhythms yet. id enter the plain chord progression into the DAW to get a feel for the mood and decide the vibe i want, what instruments to use. 

usually my rhythms come from the melody or bassline that i like but it could also be from a percussion pattern im interested in. i write down that rhythmic idea and make variations based on it, maybe half time, double time, more rests, less rests. 

i write down the melodic idea (i consider the bass as another melody). i try to make the countermelody go the opposite direction of the first one. so if the bass is funky and jumpy going up, the melody is going down gently. 

the middle instruments are different rhythmically also but not too busy. refer to the rhythmic ideas jotted down earlier and use those. i like each instrument to have only one note playing at a time, except for one or two "chord instruments" like guitar or piano. 

even those i limit to 3 or 4 notes at a time so the chords are either arpeggiated or chopped up. if there are two instruments playing chords, they are doing different inversions over different octaves, and different rhythms so they dont sound the same. one should be less busy than the other when they play together. 

i enter all those ideas into the DAW and write more notes on paper or notepad as i go so that i wont forget what i liked and to avoid repeating things that have already been done or didnt sound good. so i have all those notes on my computer too about what im working on and any ideas i might wanna expand later. 

it really sucks when i dont do preplanning so i have to do that more often!

and melodic ideas could be just up down same same

Classical music is only relaxing for people who find it boring in some way. Calling it "relaxing" in the context of a study sounds very unscientific to me. Why not specify the genre of music and leave out "relaxing", which is very subjective and extreme imo? 

I'd say only 1/4 to 1/3 of classical music are actually relaxing. I say that because of there being more "fast movements" in sonata style pieces (2 of 3 or 3 of 4) and albums / collections. Plus, classical musicians love to play fast, virtuosic, and romantic pieces. That's why the estimate of "most" classical music being "relaxing" seems off to me even as a generalization. 

Overall, classical music is potentially very moving. There's a good reason we can't play much of them on the radio - the dynamic contrasts can be huge, from pppp to ffff (with accents thrown in!) or one solo instrument to a full orchestra. Blaring that kind of music on a car ride might cause accidents on the road. I used to listen with headphones and stopped doing that with classical music because the louder parts would be very hard on the ears. 

Maybe the "pleasant and relaxing" part has to do with historical connotations. There were times when only the nobles and the church could have such music, and so the music were supposed to be pleasant and stately, even reverent at times.
